passage: The video arrived in Sarika's family group on a Tuesday morning: a well-known local doctor in Indore saying a common vaccine caused illness. Her uncle had already forwarded it to twelve people. Sarika, who worked in a newsroom, watched it twice. The lips didn't quite match the words, and the doctor's earrings changed between frames. She called her colleague Vidya, who handled fact-checks. Vidya found the original clip in ten minutes; the doctor had been talking about something else entirely. Sarika posted the original link in the family group with a gentle note. Her uncle replied, "How can you be sure?" She explained the earrings. There was a long pause, then he deleted his forward and wrote, "Thank you, beta."

qa.q: How many people had Sarika's uncle forwarded the video to?
qa.a: He had forwarded it to twelve people.

qa.q: What might her uncle's long pause before deleting the forward suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed or unsettled at having been fooled, before accepting the evidence.

qa.q: What steps did Sarika take before challenging the video?
qa.a: She watched it carefully, noticed mismatches, asked a fact-checker and found the original clip before posting.

qa.q: How might the doctor be affected by the fake video spreading?
qa.a: The doctor's reputation could be harmed and people might lose trust in real health advice.

grounding: Shows a young journalist detecting a manipulated video and verifying it before correcting family members.

passage: Last month someone sent me a voice note that sounded exactly like my friend Nazia, crying, saying she'd been arrested in Dubai and needed money fast. My heart was pounding. I actually opened my banking app. Then something small bothered me. She called me 'Jaya-ji'. Nazia has never called me that in fifteen years. I hung up and called Nazia's real number. She answered from her office in Hyderabad, confused. It was a cloned voice. I felt sick thinking how close I came. I reported the number to the cybercrime helpline and warned our friends' group. Now Nazia and I have a silly code word. It feels a bit dramatic. But I'd rather feel dramatic than fooled.

qa.q: Where was Nazia actually when Jaya called her?
qa.a: She was at her office in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What made Jaya suspicious of the voice note?
qa.a: The voice said 'Jaya-ji', which the real Nazia never does, so something felt wrong despite the panic.

qa.q: What smart steps did Jaya take after hanging up?
qa.a: Jaya called Nazia's real number, reported the scam number to the cybercrime helpline and warned their friends.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt learning her voice was cloned?
qa.a: She was probably confused and uneasy that her voice could be used to trick her friends.

Desk editor's note, fact-check team (Ritu):
On Tuesday a video spread showing a state minister apparently mocking flood victims. Three rival outlets had already posted it. Kalyani, 25, our newest fact-checker, asked for thirty minutes before we ran anything. I watched her work. She noticed the minister's lips drifted out of sync on two words, and the shadow on his collar didn't move with his head. She found the original speech on the government channel; the words weren't there. She traced the clip to an account created that week. She was nervous presenting it, since everyone else had run the story. We published a clear verification piece instead, showing each step so readers could learn to check. Two outlets later took their versions down. Next: I've asked Kalyani to run a short session for the desk on spotting synthetic video.

qa.q: How long did Kalyani ask for before the team ran anything?
qa.a: Thirty minutes.

qa.q: Why was Kalyani nervous presenting her findings?
qa.a: Everyone else had already run the story, so going against them felt risky for the newest fact-checker.

qa.q: Which verification steps did Kalyani use?
qa.a: Checking lip-sync and shadows for glitches, finding the original speech on the official channel, and tracing the clip to a newly created account.

qa.q: How might readers benefit from the verification piece?
qa.a: Seeing each step shown lets them learn how to check suspicious videos themselves before sharing.

grounding: An editor's note shows a young fact-checker detecting a synthetic video and verifying before publishing.

Wednesday night
Embarrassing day. This morning I forwarded an audio clip to the family group, a 'police officer' warning about child kidnappers in our area, sounding very official. Mausi immediately stopped sending my cousins to tuition. By lunch Anand, who works at a newspaper, messaged me: 'Tarun bhai, where did you get this? It's been doing the rounds in four states with different city names.' My stomach dropped. I searched the exact lines and found three fact-check articles calling it fake. The voice might even be generated. I'd spread panic in five minutes. So I posted a correction in the group with the links, and said sorry, especially to Mausi. She sent a folded-hands emoji, thank God. New rule for myself: if something makes me scared or angry fast, I wait and search before forwarding. That feeling is exactly what these clips want.

qa.a: Child kidnappers in their area, supposedly from a police officer.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Anand questioned the clip?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he was embarrassed and alarmed at having spread panic.

qa.q: What rule did Tarun make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: If something makes him scared or angry fast, he waits and searches before forwarding, because fake clips rely on those quick emotions.

qa.q: How did the clip affect Mausi?
qa.a: She was frightened enough to stop sending her children to tuition, until Tarun's correction reassured her.

passage: The video reached the village group chat in Buldhana district on a Sunday morning: a blurry clip of men dragging a child into a van, captioned "Kidnappers in our area. Beware of strangers." By noon two traders selling steel utensils had been surrounded near the bus stop. Tushar, who taught at the zilla parishad school, felt his stomach knot. He had seen the clip before. He searched using a still from the video and found it in a news report from another country, four years old, about a film shoot. He ran to the bus stop, where Sarpanch Ramesh was trying to calm the crowd, and showed him the old report. Ramesh read it slowly, called the police station, and told the crowd the video was fake. The traders were escorted out safely. That evening Tushar posted the original report in the group, with one line: "Please check before forwarding."

passage: Camila was three weeks into her job as a junior producer at a news website in Dublin when a photo exploded across social media: a well-known bridge over the Liffey, half underwater, cars floating. Fifty thousand shares in an hour. Her editor wanted it up. "Everyone else is running it." Liam, a senior producer, leaned over. "Check it first." Camila zoomed in. The water reflected sunlight, but the sky was grey. One car had four headlights on one side. She searched for the image and found no earlier copy and no photographer, and the flood-monitoring service showed normal river levels. She rang a council press officer, who said the bridge was dry. Camila told her editor it looked AI-generated. They ran a short piece instead: "Viral flood image is fake: here's how we checked." It became their most-read story of the week.

qa.q: How many shares did the photo get in an hour?
qa.a: Fifty thousand.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling under the editor's pressure to run it?
qa.a: Camila was probably nervous and pressured as a junior, but uneasy enough to check first.

qa.q: Which checks showed the photo was fake?
qa.a: Sunlit reflections under a grey sky, a car with four headlights on one side, no earlier copy or photographer, normal river levels, and a council officer confirming the bridge was dry.

qa.q: How might the editor see Camila's check after the story's success?
qa.a: The editor, who wanted to rush it, probably felt relieved and impressed that verifying became the week's most-read story.

grounding: A junior news producer in Ireland verifies a viral flood image as synthetic before sharing it.

The staffroom at the girls' school in Lucknow went silent when Rekha held up her phone. "Have you seen this? The principal, saying students from the basti shouldn't be admitted."

The clip was forty seconds long. Seema watched it twice. The principal's voice sounded right. But her lips seemed a little behind the words, and her earrings flickered oddly when she turned.

"Rekha, don't forward it yet," Seema said.

"Why? Everyone's already sharing it."

"Something's off with the mouth. And she said the opposite at the parents' meeting last week. I was there."

Seema found the school's own recording of that meeting and played a minute of it. Same saree, same stage, very different words. Then she called the principal's office. The principal had already heard about the fake clip and was filing a complaint.

Rekha deleted the video from her phone. "I almost sent it to my mother's group," she said quietly.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she said she almost sent it to her mother's group?
qa.a: Rekha felt embarrassed and a little shaken, realising she nearly spread a fake video.

qa.q: What steps did Seema take to verify the clip?
qa.a: She noticed the lips and earrings, compared it with the school's own recording, and called the principal's office before anyone shared it.

Dear Shankar Mama,

I saw the flood video you shared on the family group this morning, with "Today in Guwahati!! Pray!!" I know you sent it because you were worried about people there, and that's why I'm writing to you directly and not replying in the group.

I checked it. The same video is on a news site from 2019, from a different country. The shop signs are in another language if you pause it. There is no flood in Guwahati today; the weather office shows light rain.

I'm not upset. These videos are made to look urgent so people share them fast. I've nearly shared a few myself. What I do now: pause and look at signs, search a frame of it, and check one reliable news source first.

Could you delete it from the group? If you like, I'll call you on Sunday and show you how I check. It takes two minutes.

With love,
Rekha

Thanks, Rashmi. You asked about the audio clip, so, I'm Kavitha, I run the district desk, and we came very close to publishing a fake.

It arrived at 10 p.m.: a councillor's voice, apparently offering money for votes. It sounded exactly like her. Our editor wanted it up by midnight. Every other page was already sharing it.

So we waited. I called her office and the person the audio said she was speaking to. Both denied it and gave us their phone logs. We sent the file to a lab that checks voice recordings. They said it was very likely generated.

We ran a story the next day, but about the fake, and how we checked it. Our editor was grumpy for a week. But nobody had to take anything back.

Tarun called Vikas, his younger brother, directly. Vikas was at work, fine, confused. Their mother sat down shaking.

Swati, you're new to the newsroom, so let me tell you why I'm so slow to share anything.
When I was twenty-four, in my first year as a reporter, there was violence in our city. A photo came in on a group: a temple burning, supposedly that morning. Everyone was sharing it. My editor wanted it online in ten minutes.
Something bothered me. The shadows were wrong for morning. I did a reverse image search. It was from a different country, six years earlier.
If we'd published it, people could have been hurt. Crowds were already angry.
Now there are tools that can make a photo from nothing, which is worse. But the rule is the same: who took it, when, where? Can I find the original? If I can't, it doesn't run.
That's why your Ankita Didi takes the extra ten minutes, every time.

qa.q: How many years earlier had the photo really been taken?
qa.a: Six years earlier.

qa.q: How did young Ankita feel about the photo before checking?
qa.a: Young Ankita felt uneasy and suspicious because the shadows looked wrong for morning.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Doing a reverse image search mattered, because it showed the photo was old and foreign, preventing a fake from inflaming angry crowds.

qa.q: How might the editor have felt when Ankita showed the result?
qa.a: The editor was probably shaken and relieved, realising how close they came to publishing it.

grounding: Shows an elder journalist recounting how verification stopped a fake image and why it matters more with synthetic media.

passage: Afreen was at her cousin's wedding, the band so loud she could barely think, when her phone lit up. Her uncle had forwarded a video to the family group: the city's municipal commissioner announcing that tap water was contaminated and nobody should drink it for three days. Sixty relatives, forty already reacting in panic. Her battery was at eleven percent. Afreen watched it twice, holding the phone close. The commissioner's mouth moved a fraction behind the words, and the voice had no echo though he stood in a big hall. Her friend Harish, a journalist, was at the next table. "Check the corporation's official page," he said, leaning in. She did. Nothing about contamination; a notice from an hour ago said the water supply was normal. She typed in the family group, "Please don't share. Looks fake, the official page says the water is fine," and pasted the link. Then her phone died.

qa.q: What battery level did Afreen's phone have?
qa.a: Her battery was at eleven percent.

qa.q: What was Afreen probably feeling while watching the video at the wedding?
qa.a: She was likely alarmed and suspicious, watching it twice and noticing the lips lagging behind the words 😰

qa.q: Which steps helped Afreen stop the rumour?
